entries.title: How GitHub Used AI to Port Copilot From TypeScript to Rust in Record Time
entries.summary: In this article, we’ll look at how this porting was done and the learnings along the way.
entries.content:
NYSE President Lynn Martin discusses AI (Sponsored)

AI is moving fast, from experiments to agents that act on their own. Few people have a better view of what that shift means for business than Lynn Martin, President of NYSE Group. At the Agentic Data Summit on December 9, Lynn joins Redpanda Founder & CEO Alex Gallego for a conversation on what it takes to adopt AI where reliability is everything, how AI is showing up in the companies coming to market, and why timely, trustworthy data matters more than ever as agents start acting in real time. Tune in at 9:19 AM PT. The summit is free and virtual and runs 8:30 AM–2:00 PM PT.

GitHub recently rewrote the software engine behind multiple Copilot products. They ported the codebase from TypeScript to Rust. Almost 800K lines of code. And the great part was that all of this was done using the GitHub Copilot app itself.

This porting exercise was triggered because the existing design was eating up a lot of resources. It was also becoming difficult to embed Copilot in other applications.

However, a project of this size would have required a big team of developers and a couple of years to get done. But by using the GitHub Copilot app, Copilot CLI, and AI agents, a single developer was able to finish the whole thing in a few months. In this article, we’ll look at how this porting was done and the learnings along the way. Here’s what we will cover:

  • The need for porting the Copilot runtime

  • The porting strategy

  • How the porting work started

  • The role of agent fleets

  • How the new code was reviewed

  • What were the issues

  • The performance impact

  • Cost of porting and learnings

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

The Need for Porting the Copilot Runtime

You can think of GitHub’s Copilot runtime as the shared software engine that takes care of AI agent behavior across multiple products. Due to this runtime, all these products can reuse the same capabilities instead of needing to maintain their own implementation.

Originally, the GitHub engineering team had built the runtime using TypeScript that ran on Node and the V8 JavaScript engine. While this supported rapid development, the runtime was tightly coupled to the command-line application’s user interface. When GitHub needed an SDK to let other applications talk to Copilot, it built that SDK on top of the existing command-line application. When you started the SDK client, you had to launch a separate background process that was made up of the command-line application and its runtime. Requests and responses moved between the consumer app and that process.

This setup became harder to justify when the runtime spread to applications that had stricter requirements for speed, memory usage, and scale. Even if you had an application written in Python, Java, or C#, it had to hold the additional Node and V8 machinery. When you started a client, you had to launch another process and prepare JavaScript for execution. Each client had to bear roughly 100 MB of memory overhead at a bare minimum. Also, processes talking to each other added a lot of overhead. Lastly, applications had to monitor two processes, and a crash in the Node process could take the session with it. These costs were a huge problem for services that hosted many clients.

Therefore, GitHub wanted a standalone runtime library that was clearly separate from the UI. Applications should be able to load that library directly into their own process.

Rust was an ideal choice for this type of requirement. It had low overhead and predictable resource usage. An early estimate showed that roughly 130K lines of production TypeScript had to be ported. But additional logic moved out of the interface layer into the runtime. Also, you had other developers adding new features. Ultimately, 430K lines of production TypeScript code moved through the migration.

How much of your week is spent answering questions? (Sponsored)

New hires, support, PMs, and your coding agents all need to know how the product works and why it works that way. Today, you’re the one pointing them in the right direction.

Unblocked works out what’s current and relevant across your code, PRs, tickets, Slack, and production data, so:

  • Everyone gets cited answers in Slack without pulling in an engineer

  • When the answer turns into a fix, a cloud agent drafts the PR

  • Your agents generate code that follows past decisions, no steering needed

The Porting Strategy

GitHub used an incremental, in-place porting strategy.

In this strategy, you replace the runtime one piece at a time, even when the product is under active development. The development team could continue to add new features and release updates throughout the migration.

The GitHub engineering team didn’t go for a complete rewrite followed by one large switchover. This approach would have concentrated all the risk into a single release. The replacement would need to keep catching up with oncoming changes. With the smaller replacements, they were able to make each change easier to review, test, and investigate.

The process worked in a step-by-step manner. A component’s TypeScript implementation was replaced with Rust in a single pull request, which grouped the changes for review. Any TypeScript code that depended on that component called the new Rust implementation through a thin wrapper. You can think of this wrapper as a temporary bridge between two languages. The old implementation was deleted as part of the same change, so that the team had to maintain only one active version of the component. As more and more stuff moved to Rust, these temporary bridges were also removed.

As far as the tasks were concerned, the work began with small, independent helpers that already had strong test suites and didn’t manage shared state. These early changes also helped test the build setup, packaging, and communication between languages. Once they had made the approach concrete, the migration went to more interconnected parts of the system.

Throughout this process, the key aim was to maintain existing behavior and algorithms. Broader redesigns were pushed after migration. At each step, validation was performed. They had existing end-to-end tests that checked if complete workflows behaved properly as their implementation changed. If there was a test failure, the changes weren’t merged. Also, when it came to the users, the ported components reached users through incremental releases. They often appeared in a pre-release before going to a stable release.

How the Porting Work Started

GitHub started with a few small, working examples to test the waters before dealing with larger components.

The first couple of pull requests took care of the basic Rust setup. Things like build tools, automated checks, and coding instructions. They also introduced the runtime library and mechanisms for TypeScript and Rust to talk to each other.

The first main porting change moved three independent helper functions through the complete process. You can think of these early efforts as checking whether the translated code worked well. The team also tested how Rust code would be organized, built, packaged, and integrated with existing code. This gave the team practical experience with the entire process.

The rest of the work was ordered according to dependencies. For example, you had small helpers and supporting utilities come first. It was followed by components that managed state, then tools, model clients, and other integrations.

Session orchestration, which is supposed to manage much of the runtime, was left for the end. This is because larger subsystems often needed several rounds of work.

The Role of Agent Fleets

Agent fleets played a key role in dividing the migration work among multiple AI agents working at the same time. You could have a coordinating agent investigate a large component, break the work into smaller tasks, and create other agents to handle them. The Copilot app made it possible to check these sessions and switch between them. It also let them exchange messages as the work progressed.

The team got two different types of assistance from these agents. First, you had the subagents that worked within the parent session’s workspace and returned their findings to it. These subagents were good for investigating code and answering specific questions. Then, you had the child sessions that had their own Git branches and separate working copies of the repository. This lets them make changes independently. This separation helped multiple agents work on different areas of the implementation without any risk.

One example was around the session[dot].ts file that was roughly 30K lines and connected to many parts of the runtime. The coordinating agent spent an hour reading and checking before creating anything. After analyzing, it divided the work among 15 child sessions. It made the choice of models for each task. The parent talked with these sessions and tracked their progress from beginning to end. Finally, it brought the completed changes into its own branch.

Despite the advantages, running so many agents also created some limitations. When all 15 sessions tried to build and test their code at the same time, they overwhelmed the developer’s laptop. The workflow was adjusted so that child agents avoided expensive builds and tests. All that work was left for the parent. A separate chat session took care of build access for each of the porting sessions. It only allowed one build at a time.

Much of the agent fleet’s activities involved reading code, checking for dependencies, testing, and reviewing results. Their role wasn’t limited to writing Rust code. They also helped understand the existing system and check whether the replacement kept the same behavior. During all of this, human oversight remained critical.

How the New Code was Reviewed

Developers were constantly changing the repository, and hence, code review had to check both the translation and whether the port had the latest changes. The team used a reusable instruction called “rust-rebase-review” to handle this process.

First, the main agent pushed its work to the latest main branch and resolved any conflicts. After this, it checked that any newly incoming TypeScript changes had also been ported into Rust. Deleting the old TypeScript helped bring such changes to attention. If another developer modified a deleted file, Hit would flag a conflict that had to be handled.

Next, you had multiple review agents using different AI models compare the old TypeScript with the new Rust code line by line. Their main job was to identify changes in behavior or compatibility. They also checked whether the Rust implementation was efficient enough. Also, whether obsolete TypeScript and temporary wrappers had been removed. They also had to ensure that existing end-to-end tests remained unchanged because they were the only reference for expected behavior.

The code review was done in a repeated cycle. When agents found any issues, the coordinating agent checked the findings and fixed any valid problems. This continued until the reviews became clean. Every round of fixes could be committed and pushed so automated checks could be done along with further reviews. Copilot Code Review and additional review bots also checked every commit and left feedback on the pull request.

Human reviewers focused on architecture, interface contracts, and risk factors that might have been highlighted by agents or tests.

What Were the Issues

The porting exercise caused some regressions as well. You can think of these regressions as behavior that had worked earlier but stopped working as expected after the rewrite. The team found and fixed a bunch of regressions.

A common problem was that translated code changed the existing behaviour in a subtle manner. For example, some whole-number values were changed to decimal numbers, causing issues with certain SDKs. Other differences were around empty strings, time zones, or replacement libraries that had a different way of handling errors. The code could compile successfully. But the results could not be handled by other parts of the system.

Another major group of issues was around state management and coordination of operations. For example, when an operation was cancelled, it didn’t always stop all the related work. Also, when resources were released too early, the session got stuck. There was also a loss of some features. And some of them were only partially migrated.

There were also general integration and performance problems. For example, the Rust code sometimes performed lengthy work on Node’s main thread. This froze the interface. On Windows, missing process-launch settings made unwanted console windows appear.

The Performance Impact of Porting

The rewrite brought down the overhead of running Copilot’s agent runtime. Especially in terms of time and memory. With the use of Rust, there was no need to initialize Node and V8. Also, no need to load and prepare the JavaScript application. Applications could load the Rust runtime directly into their own process. This avoided the cost of talking with a separate runtime process.

GitHub saw performance gains during their detailed testing. For example, in a particular trial, creating a client, completing a single turn, and cleaning up took 5.25 seconds before the porting and 292 milliseconds after porting. This was an improvement of almost 18 times.

They also had capacity gains. In a test where many sessions shared one client, throughput went up from 7.55 completed session lifecycles per second to 120. Memory consumption also went down. In a 10-client test, the peak increase in private memory went down from 1383 MB to 126 MB.

The rewrite largely preserved the original algorithms. More improvements could happen if parts of the runtime are redesigned around Rust’s approach to memory ownership and concurrency.

Cost of Porting and Learnings

The entire porting work cost around $120K in AI token costs. They covered roughly 136 billion tokens. Most of this volume was made up of cached input, which brought down the cost of repeatedly processing existing context.

More than that, you also had developer time that was spent on this work. Apart from the main developer, other developers also made contributions to integrations, packaging, build improvements, and reviews.

There were a lot of learnings along the way.

For one, it was critical to give clear instructions to the AI tools. Some of the initial requests to port a component sometimes led agents to translate only the central logic. The surrounding work stayed in TypeScript. The instructions had to be made more effective to handle this.

Another learning was that to perform such a migration successfully, you need strong end-to-end tests. These tests should check if complete workflows retained their original behavior. The team improved its test coverage beforehand. But additional coverage could have prevented some more regressions.

The tests also needed protection. For example, you don’t want an agent changing an implementation to make the test weaker or alter an expected result. So, you need to have some sort of oversight.

One more learning was that for such migrations, you should try to translate things first without worrying about redesigning. It’s more important to keep existing behavior and algorithms intact. If you attempt to combine the porting with other improvements, it only increases issues, time, and token costs.

entries.summary: Most of its reviews are posted before the first human reviewer even opens the PR
entries.content:
4 Key Insights for Scaling LLM Applications (Sponsored)

The challenge of running LLM applications in production is that failures are silent, costs are unpredictable, and security vulnerabilities are hard to detect until it’s too late.

Download this Datadog eBook for practical strategies to monitor, debug, and secure your LLM application workflows end-to-end. You’ll get 4 key insights into how to overcome the challenges of deploying LLMs at scale — from tracing multi-step chain executions and detecting prompt injection attacks to tracking token costs and evaluating output quality in real time.

LinkedIn has more than 10,000 active code repositories, with tens of thousands of pull requests (PRs) being opened each week [1]. As coding agents write more of that code, the slow part of shipping software has moved from writing code to reviewing it.

To overcome the code review bottleneck, LinkedIn built its own AI reviewer. In a typical week, this in-house reviewer covers more than 40,000 PRs, and most of its reviews are posted before the first human reviewer even opens the PR [1].

To better understand the landscape of AI reviewers and how LinkedIn built theirs, we interviewed Min Chen, a Principal Staff Engineer at LinkedIn, and Balaji Srinivasan, Senior Director of Engineering at LinkedIn. Thanks to both of them for their time and for being open about what did not work.

In this article, you’ll learn:

  • What an AI code reviewer is, and why review is the bottleneck these days

  • Three main directions for teams and companies to handle the code review bottleneck

  • How to build a multi-agent AI reviewing system that works in production

  • What evaluation looks like for AI reviewers

  • What’s ahead and where the new bottlenecks move

What Is an AI Code Reviewer?

Software development has two main steps. An engineer writes a change, and other engineers review it before it merges into the main codebase.

When an engineer writes the code, the change becomes a PR. Then reviewers read its diff, that is, the lines it adds, removes, or changes. Here are the typical steps from when a writer opens a PR to when the PR is merged back into the codebase:

  • The author opens a PR from a branch that has the change.

  • The code host, such as GitHub, notifies the reviewers and starts continuous integration (CI), which runs tests and linters (to flag style problems and simple errors).

  • A reviewer reads the PR and comments on specific lines.

  • The author pushes fixes. Then the reviewer looks again.

  • The reviewer approves, and the PR merges.

AI is changing this development process, because it can now help with some of these steps. Engineers hand those steps to AI agents and spend more of their time focusing on intent and judgement. That is AI-native development.

Specifically for the writing step, frontier coding agents have shown promise lately. Given a task, an agent implements the feature, writes the tests, then runs those tests, and iterates until they pass. Finally, it opens a PR for review.

With coding agents, writing (the first step) can now be largely automated and done much faster. Instead of an engineer spending hours or days writing a change, the agent spends minutes writing it. But if real humans still have to review the proposed changes, the process will still be slow, because engineers’ hours are still fixed and limited.

The fix is a system that can reliably review code, ideally before humans do. That system is called an AI reviewer. It reads a PR the way a human reviewer would and comments on the lines that need attention. Once the automated code review is complete, the author, in this case the coding agent, addresses them so human reviewers spend their limited time on judging the fixes.

Since models are also getting better at reading code, more teams are automating reviews this way [2]. They mostly differ in the extent to which they aim to automate the reviewing process. Full automation would let AI approve changes on its own. This is difficult, and most labs are not there yet.

Partial automation keeps human approval on changes and gives AI the first pass. This makes the process faster but keeps real humans in the loop to reduce the risk of merging buggy or insecure code. Partial automation is more feasible these days, and companies that have an AI reviewer in place, like LinkedIn, usually use partial automation. In the rest of this article, we focus on partial automation.

But why is building an AI reviewer challenging? For an AI reviewer to be reliable, it has to have four properties:

  • Grounded: it flags real problems in the changed lines.

  • High-signal: the issues it produces are real bugs and high-risk lines (not just minor style nits a linter would catch).

  • Codebase-aware: it follows the codebase’s own conventions.

  • Timely: it comments while the author can still act on it.

Getting all four at once is the hard part. LinkedIn built its own system over several iterations to get there. Let’s see how they built it.

Stop reinstalling your toolchain on every CI run (Sponsored)

AI agents open more pull requests, and each one reinstalls the same dependencies from scratch. That is wasted CI time and money.

  • The WarpBuild cache restores dependencies between jobs

  • Twice as fast at half the cost of default runners

Trusted by teams at Braintrust, Raycast, OpenRouter, Comcast and Jane Street.

How to Build an AI Code Reviewer

Remember from earlier that the goal is partial automation. PRs still get a human review, but the AI review comes first. As a company, you have different options to have an AI reviewer in place. Some options are easier to set up but less flexible, while others take more work to build but give you more control over the quality of the comments.

Three common directions are:

  • Use a vendor’s reviewer

  • Use an off-the-shelf model with your rules

  • Build a custom multi-agent review system

Direction 1: Use a vendor’s reviewer

A fast way to have an AI reviewer in place is to simply buy a hosted system from a vendor. The reviewer connects to the code host and comments on each new PR moving forward. So you don’t have to build the system internally.

This direction is simple to set up, does not need any particular expertise, and is probably the fastest option. But it has two major limits. First, it is generic. You can add a rule file, but the vendor controls the prompts and the harness, so many comments are generic and could apply to any project.

The second limit is control. The vendor owns the system, so it decides when the model or the instructions change. You cannot test an update before engineers see it or gradually roll out a change.

LinkedIn tried this option first. During an AI-native pilot, teams were asked to opt in to a vendor’s hosted reviewer. But the team observed that the comments were noisy and generic. They did not fit LinkedIn’s codebase and each repository’s rules. When the comments are noisy, engineers lose trust.

Soon, engineers asked to opt out, which meant the full manual review was back again. The team also had no control over the vendor’s changes. Min put it this way: “You don’t own anything. They do something, they change something, you just react to it.”

Direction 2: Use an off-the-shelf model with your rules

Since a hosted reviewer is too generic, a natural next step is to use an off-the-shelf model, but build your own harness around it. That way, you can choose your own prompts and write the codebase’s own rules into its instructions. With those instructions and more control over the harness, the comments will be more specific to your conventions.

This direction sounds promising: the comments would be specific to the codebase and would likely arrive quickly, before human review. But it has two main problems.

The first problem is hallucination. Because the system relies on a single model and there is no verification in place, if the model hallucinates, nothing will catch it. The author will end up with a comment about a problem that does not exist, or a real problem attached to the wrong line.

The second problem is knowledge gaps. A model learns what good and bad code look like from its training data. With a single model, it will work well on areas that overlap with its training data, but will fail on out-of-distribution inputs or inputs that were less frequent in the training data. That means a single reviewer model misses the same classes of issues repeatedly and may over-flag the same low-value issues.

LinkedIn also observed the same issues when the team built the review system with their repository-specific rules. The model gave good results but produced many hallucinations, and some of its comments did not even match the line numbers in the diff. Using a different model for review than for writing code did not fix the hallucination issue. But that idea led the team to ask whether a second model could check and verify the first model, the idea behind the multi-agent design.

Direction 3: Build a custom multi-agent review system

This direction relies on multiple agents to produce grounded reviews. There are different design patterns for multi-agent systems, but a popular one is the orchestrator-subagent pattern [3], where one agent hands work to several subagents and combines their results. For code review, the subagents independently review the same PR, often each with a different model, and return their findings with line numbers. The orchestrator then merges overlapping findings, ranks them by confidence, and posts only reliable reviews.

This design can mitigate most of the limitations of the previous directions because you own the whole system, different models cover each other’s knowledge gaps, and findings by different agents must be verified by others to survive and be posted.

To add your rules and codebase conventions, there are two ways. One is context injection, which means adding a rule file to the repository that the AI reviewer reads on every PR. This can work in simple codebases, but is not a flexible approach because some rules apply to every repository, some to one repository, and some to one kind of change. A single file being injected as context cannot contain all three or combine the right ones for each PR.

The other approach, which LinkedIn used, is a layered design. You design several tiers, and each has its own scope, owner, and rules. Then a dedicated subagent uses those rules to perform an independent review. LinkedIn used the following three tiers:

  • Company-wide rules apply to every repository. These can be YAML files clarifying what the model should check.

  • Repository rules cover one codebase. This can be a markdown file containing the team’s conventions like coding standards and review criteria.

  • Pull request rules apply only to one kind of change.

To better understand how this system reviews a PR, let’s go over a concrete example and see how each step handles it. Imagine an author opens a PR that has a new python file named cache.py, implementing an in-memory cache for a Python service. But the code has two problems. It has a race condition and a bare except.

The author, who may be a coding agent, writes the change and opens a PR. The PR is then handed to the AI reviewer, which reviews it in the following three steps.

Step 1: Running parallel independent reviews

The orchestrator fetches the diff and codebase context, then dispatches them to several subagents at once. A subagent builds its own prompt, reviews the full diff in the context of the codebase and its recent changes, and then returns its structured findings.

Notice that the subagents never see each other’s findings while they review. If Subagent A could read Subagent B’s findings first, it would tend to agree, but because the subagents work independently, their agreement counts as evidence.

Step 2: Merging reviews

The independent subagents from the previous step produce findings. Many of those findings may overlap, pointing to the same issue(s). For example, if three subagents find the same five issues, the author gets fifteen comments for five problems. So the orchestrator has to merge duplicates.

This can be done in two phases. First, a deterministic check marks findings with overlapping line ranges as candidates, a cheap step that limits the search to the same code. Second, an LLM decides whether each candidate pair describes the same problem. This second phase is necessary to find overlaps semantically because two models usually do not phrase an issue the same way.

The overlaps also indicate review confidence. If multiple findings merge into a single comment, the engineer is more likely to accept it, so the code reviewer can rank it higher.

The outcome of this step is a shorter list of findings, with overlapping ones merged into single high-confidence comments. However, we still need to check the findings that only one subagent raised, which is the focus of the last step.

Step 3: Verifying reviews

A finding from only one subagent is harder to judge. It might be a real issue the other model missed, but it might also be a hallucination. To find out, the orchestrator sends those to another model to verify against the code. According to LinkedIn’s post, this often saves real issues [1]. A model that missed an issue, when asked to verify another model’s finding, confirms the issue is real. Verified findings are then rated for importance.

When the verifying model contradicts the finding, its confidence score drops. Then, low-scoring findings become candidates for filtering. In addition, findings that are cosmetic, already fixed in a later commit, or against the repository’s established patterns are suppressed before posting.

With multiple agents, layered rules, and a three-step workflow, the system has all the properties we described earlier. It merges several independent reviews into one, verifies the findings, and posts the review.

How to Evaluate an AI Code Reviewer

Labs and teams owning an AI reviewer system constantly change it. They may swap models, edit prompts, or add something in the harness. To tell whether a change will make the AI reviewer better, you must run evaluations, or evals, which are repeatable tests of an AI reviewer’s quality.

In this section, we cover the two phases of running evals for an AI reviewer: before a change is released, and in production after the code merges.

Eval before a release

Before a change ships, you need to know whether the change will improve things or not. A typical process is to run the production version and the candidate on the same PRs and compare their reviews, either with an LLM judge or against a golden dataset built from human labels.

With an LLM judge, a separate model takes both reviews of the same PR as inputs, and scores them. This is cheap to run and does not need human labels. You mostly need to have a fixed rubric so the LLM follows a more predictable and reliable path to score the reviews. LinkedIn has a rubric with six weighted yes-or-no criteria, and runs every prompt, model, and harness change through this before they ship.

LLM-as-a-judge works well for comparisons [4], but it cannot reliably decide which comments are actually right. A golden dataset fills that gap with known right answers.

A typical process is to collect real PRs at the point a bug was found, and humans mark which review comments are correct. This becomes our golden dataset. We can score candidates against these labels and measure traditional metrics like precision and recall. LinkedIn has built such a dataset and is now building the eval on top of it, as a complement to its LLM-as-a-judge.

Eval in production

Pre-release evals run on a sample of PRs or a fixed dataset, so they cannot show how the reviewer performs on thousands of real PRs, or whether engineers find its comments useful. Those kinds of measurements can be obtained only from production. Evaluating an AI reviewer in production relies on two things: the right metrics and a feedback loop.

The right metrics determine how well your system is doing in production. There are often so many different metrics to track, such as time to first review, cost per review, and how engineers react to comments. But some are more insightful than others. Emoji reactions, for example, are noisy because they say little about whether a comment helped. On the other hand, acceptance rate is a good metric because it checks whether the code changed because of a comment. Balaji explained what counts as acceptance at LinkedIn: “Not someone giving thumbs up or thumbs down, but the code actually changed.”

LinkedIn evaluated their system in production and measured acceptance on thousands of AI comments. As the next figure shows, engineers accepted 63.9% of them [1]. These numbers show that engineers act on most of the AI reviewer’s comments, with the highest rates on concurrency bugs and dead code (100%) and logic errors (80%).

We talked about metrics, but the more important part of evaluation in production is to have a feedback loop: a mechanism that turns those measurements into actual fixes.

As you measure your system with different metrics, you learn where the gaps are. If you run and measure your system every day, you can close those gaps. For example, LinkedIn now runs its acceptance check daily and produces a trend report of which rules and prompts are gaining or losing acceptance. The team uses it to decide which rules to disable and which prompts to change.

That is evaluation. Pre-release evals check whether a change is safe to ship, and the daily loop measures the system in production and improves it over time.

What’s Next

In Balaji’s view, the next bottleneck after review is confidence in the quality of the software as a whole, which takes more than reviewing each PR. He does not expect review to stop being a bottleneck until automated validation is in place. Deploying, monitoring, and handling incidents also take more effort than development, so LinkedIn is aiming AI tools there too. As he put it, “the faster we are pushing out code, the faster we are potentially breaking production.”

LinkedIn’s next step for its AI reviewer is a risk heat map: an optional feature that will score each region of a PR’s diff by predicted risk so that engineers review the riskiest parts first.

References

[1] High-Signal AI Code Review That Adapts to Your Codebase at Scale: https://www.linkedin.com/blog/engineering/ai/high-signal-ai-code-review-that-adapts-to-your-codebase-at-scale

[2] 60 million Copilot code reviews and counting: https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/60-million-copilot-code-reviews-and-counting/

[3] How we built our multi-agent research system: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system

[4] Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena: https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685

entries.summary: Orchestration in an AI system manages tasks across agents, handles failures, shared memory and context.
entries.content:
A state-of-the-art, fully assembled agent harness (Sponsored)

Match or beat harnesses on accuracy with 28% fewer tokens. Strands harness is open source and ships with benchmarked defaults for the system prompt, tools, memory, sessions, and context management, so you can skip wiring up a harness piece by piece.

Spin it up from the CLI or in a few lines of Python or TypeScript. Nothing is a black box: swap model providers, override any default, or drop down to the SDK primitives with no rewrite. Then validate before you ship with 25+ built-in evaluators.

From idea to production with fewer tokens wasted.

This week’s system design refresher:

  • 6 frequently used orchestration frameworks in an AI system

  • Top 6 Cost Optimization Strategies in AI Systems

  • How a SQL Query Executes Inside a Database

  • How does a request actually travel through Claude Code?

6 frequently used orchestration frameworks in an AI system

Orchestration in an AI system manages tasks across agents, handles failures, shared memory and context.

  • LangGraph: This uses a graph-based technique where workflows are represented as nodes and edges determine the state transitions.

  • CrewAI: A role-based abstraction technique is used here. Agents are assigned a defined role and goal that enables them to work on the tasks sequentially or via a manager agent .

  • Microsoft Agent Framework: This framework is designed to handle organizational workflows. It also uses graphs with built-in branching, checkpoints, and human intervention pauses.

  • OpenAI Agents SDK: An LLM driven runtime approach is used, where an agent decides whether it should delegate control to other agent or retain execution to complete the task itself.

  • Google ADK: Hybrid control approach is used where a developer defines a strategy to run tasks and a root agent splits and distributes tasks to sub-agents.

  • Claude Agent SDK: No separate layer for orchestration exists. It lives inside an agent which gathers context, works with tools, evaluates and keeps going until no calls left.

Top 6 Cost Optimization Strategies in AI Systems

Your AI bills can grow quickly. The diagram below shows the top 6 techniques to make your AI system less expensive.

Prompt caching: This technique caches stable prefixes like system prompts and tool schemas. This means the model can skip redundant computation on requests with a shared prefix.

Model routing: A router sends simple queries to a small model and hard requests to a frontier model. Since a lot of queries are simple in practice, this can save a lot of money.

Batch API: This technique processes large jobs asynchronously by batching the requests first and then sending them. Providers often offer discounts on batch requests.

Semantic cache: We use an embedding model to cache queries. When there is a hit, the stored answer will be reused instead of calling the model again.

Trim the context: This technique trims the conversation history. This prevents sending the whole conversation every time, which can be costly.

Smaller model: We can also use techniques like distillation or quantization to convert a large model into a smaller model.

Over to you: Which of these techniques are most useful in production?

INFER/CON: Meet the People Building the AI Stack (Sponsored)

Join AI engineers, researchers, founders, and technical leaders at INFER/CON on November 16 in San Francisco. Convened by Datadog, this one-day conference brings together speakers from Anthropic, Together AI, Inferact, Fireworks AI, and more. Explore inference performance, production reliability, evaluation, and the economics of AI alongside the people building and operating these systems. Expect technical conversations, practical perspectives, and opportunities to connect with peers tackling similar challenges.

Attendance is free and by application only; all applications are subject to approval.

Use exclusive code to apply: Byte/VIP

How a SQL Query Executes Inside a Database

Parse and validate: The database parses the SQL to check it is syntactically correct and the referenced objects, columns, and data types are valid. It converts the SQL into a logical query tree.

Rewrite and Transform: The database simplifies and restructures the query tree so it can be executed efficiently.

Optimize and choose a plan: The database evaluates the most efficient way to run the query. It compares different execution plans and selects the best plan that is supposed to use the least time and resources.

Execute the plan tree: The database runs the selected plan operations, like filtering, joining, and sorting, typically from the bottom of the parse tree to the top to produce the results.

Access cache and storage: The database retrieves the required data during execution from the cache when it is available or reads from the storage when it is not.

Return rows: The final result is formatted and sent back to the client.

How does a request actually travel through Claude Code?

Most of us type a prompt and watch the magic happen. The diagram below shows what's really going on behind the curtain, based on the Claude Code source code.

Let's trace one real request: "Fix the failing test in auth.test.ts."

Step 1: The user sends a prompt to Claude Code through their interface.

Step 2: The interface (CLI, IDE, or SDK) wraps the prompt with repo and file context and hands it to the agent loop as a request.

Step 3: The agent loop plans the next move and proposes an action: Edit(auth.ts, lines 42–58).

Step 4: The permission system checks the proposed action against the rules.

Step 5: The approved action becomes a tool call: Edit(auth.ts, patch), dispatched to the matching tool.

Step 6: The tool runs in the execution environment (shell, cloud, or sandbox) as a real syscall.

Step 7: The execution returns a tool result back to the agent loop.

Step 8: The agent persists the turn to state and streams the final message to the user.

The whole system is just this loop, repeated until the model stops asking for tools.

Over to you: which step in this loop do you think is the hardest one to get right when building your own coding agent?

entries.title: The Hidden Work Behind Every Database Request
entries.summary: Read amplification, write amplification, and space amplification show the differences between logical work and physical cost.
entries.content:
Mostly, an application’s storage system has to do work only when users make requests to that application.

However, there’s a difference between the work requested and the work that the storage system has to perform. A storage system does extra work as well, which is equally important. It can help you find data quickly, recover data after a crash, or support concurrent transactions. But this extra work also has a cost. For example, the request might involve reading a small record, but it can require fetching many blocks of data. Or when the user requests an update to some value, it can trigger multiple writes in the storage system. Also, if you want to keep the dataset highly available, it might require much more space than the actual size of the dataset.

Read amplification, write amplification, and space amplification show the differences between logical work and physical cost. In this article, we’re going to look at these differences in detail. Here’s what we will cover:

  • What is logical work and physical work in a database

  • Read amplification

  • Write amplification

  • Space amplification

  • The amplifications with B-trees

  • The amplifications with LSM trees

  • How indexes and filters use space to avoid reads

  • How compression helps improve amplifications

  • The role of caching

  • The impact of amplification

entries.title: How Anthropic Redesigned Source Control
entries.summary: In this article, we’ll look at the architecture behind Scion.
entries.content:
A Pile of MCP Connectors Is Not a Context Engine (Sponsored)

Your team connected Slack, Jira and GitHub over MCP, and engineers still spend their time steering agents to the right answer. This article looks at why: connectors fetch from one tool at a time, so every agent stitches the pieces together itself, trusts the first doc that looks right, and adds a search to your token bill each time.

Read what changes when a context engine sits on top of your connectors: the same coding task finished 83% faster at 48% lower cost.

Anthropic has recently reached a point where coding isn’t the bottleneck for them. Claude is able to do a lot of heavy lifting. It can iterate on research loops. Or optimize complex programs. Or even build new services from scratch.

However, the main problem Anthropic faces is that the infrastructure they have around writing code is not able to keep up with the amount of code being generated by its agents. Activities like downloading repositories, preparing workspaces, and recording changes are becoming major bottlenecks.

To solve this problem, the Anthropic engineering team built Scion. You can think of Scion as a source control system that has been designed around a huge repository and clients that are almost always online. In this article, we’ll look at the architecture behind Scion. Here’s what we will cover:

  • How source control works

  • Anthropic’s problem with source control

  • Why Git couldn’t solve the problem

  • How Scion works

  • How changes are handled in Scion

  • How Scion caches data

  • How Anthropic scales Scion

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

How Source Control Works

As you will already know, a software project is made up of files that change continuously. Developers add features. They correct mistakes and update dependencies. They also sometimes need to recover an earlier version. A source control system records all these changes and lets multiple developers work on the same codebase.

Let’s look at a few key terms related to source control.

A repository contains the project’s versioned information. Next, you have a commit that denotes a specific version along with other details such as the author, a description, and a history of the earlier commits.

A branch is used to demarcate a line of development. For example, your main branch signifies the line of code into which you integrate all the reviewed and approved changes. Different developers can work on different branches and combine their code through a merge process.

The files present on a developer’s machine are known as the working copy. A checkout process prepares those files for a specific version.

Lastly, you also have automated systems that rely on source control. Continuous integration (CI) runs processes such as compilation, testing, and other checks when code changes. Each job may need a workspace that contains the appropriate version of the code. Coding agents and research jobs need similar environments.

Anthropic’s Problem with Source Control

Anthropic stores a large amount of its code in a monorepo. You can think of a monorepo as a shared repository that contains multiple projects and components. This way, code that is related can share a common history. But it also means that many separate activities might depend on the same source control infrastructure.

But a large repository is only a part of the story. Anthropic’s problem is much deeper. They report that merged changes have grown from roughly 2500 per day in May 2026 to more than 30000 per day by September. Meanwhile, the size of its main branch’s history is close to 100 GB. Even a compressed working copy goes beyond 25 GB.

The CI system is doing approximately 25 million checkouts per day. This number is before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. To be clear, you shouldn’t think of these checkouts as individual code changes. A single change can spawn many jobs. And each job prepares an environment for doing its work. Ultimately, your infrastructure workload can get much larger than the number of changes being merged.

For example, a naive approach to transfer a compressed working copy for every CI checkout can generate more than 600 PB of traffic per day. Therefore, the practical problem Anthropic faces has two sides. One is that the system must be able to accept new changes quickly. Second, it must be able to distribute the code to a huge number of consumers. If you improve only one aspect, the other can become a bottleneck.

Why Git Couldn’t Solve the Problem

The local independence of Git becomes quite expensive in this type of workload. As you might know, Git is designed in a way that an ordinary full clone of the codebase can be used as a self-contained repository.

When the necessary data is locally available, you can use Git to inspect history, compare versions, and create commits without the need to contact a central service. This is a great strength of Git.

However, Anthropic’s workload is such that this independence is not valuable. Most of the clients are automated jobs and agents that already depend on network services. At the same time, if you give those clients a good chunk of repository data, it leads to repeated transfer, storage, and maintenance costs.

To be clear, Git also has ways to reduce those costs. Anthropic used a bunch of these strategies. For example, they use features like shallow clones, sparse checkouts, partial clones, internal mirrors, and repository seeds. Each of these techniques can handle different parts of the problem. For example, a feature like sparse checkout helps deal with files that are part of the workspace.

The first architecture Anthropic built was around the use of Git. You had jobs start from seeds, obtain additional data through caches, and use layers of repository mirrors. At its peak, the Anthropic engineering team was operating several hundred internal mirrors to distribute traffic. But they had to keep all these mirrors in sync with each other as the repository data changed. Seeds also became outdated as the rate of merging increased. Operations that needed historical data became a lot harder to manage because clients held only partial repository data.

The Anthropic team realized that its workflow already had one authoritative shared repository while the infrastructure supported a lot of independence at the client level. With Scion, they changed this responsibility allocation approach.

How Scion Works

Scion makes the server responsible for repository operations. It assumes that clients can reach a source control service when they need data.

In this setup, the server answers historical data queries, calculates diffs, and creates commits. It also performs merges and rebases. The client (known as scn) maintains a limited cache and prepares files on disk. It watches for local filesystem changes and provides an interface for developers and jobs to deal with the service.

This setup is known as the client-server asymmetry. You can think of it as the client and server having different capabilities and responsibilities. For example, let’s say you have a tool that needs to find out the change behind a particular line of code. This operation is commonly known as blame. In Scion’s operating model, the tool asks the service for the answer to its question. It doesn’t need to assemble enough local history to calculate the answer.

The same principle applies when you’ve to create changes. In Git, you have a commit that’s created locally and later shared through a push. In Scion, you create a commit using a server operation. There’s no separate push step.

You might think that such a centralized service uses a single server that contains everything. But that’s not the case. Anthropic distributes the data and scales the service across machines. There’s no fully materialized repository on any single individual server. The tradeoff is that you have a strong dependence on service availability and connectivity.

How Changes are Handled by Scion

Changesets provide a small, durable record of each change. Once you create a commit on the server, you need to ensure that they are accepted efficiently.

Scion’s basic unit for managing this is a changeset. You can think of this changeset as a durable record of a change. You can easily construct other useful representations of the repository from this changeset.

To understand its structure, two terms are important. First is a blob that stores the contents of the file. Second is a tree that describes the contents of the directory. It connects names to files and subdirectories. In Git, a commit points to a root tree that represents the project at that version.

A Scion changeset records the files that changed relative to its first parent. This happens together with a reference to their contents. For example, let’s say you have a change that updates a file named “docs/guide[dot]md”, deletes “src/legacy[dot]rs, and modifies “tools/build[dot]sh”. The changeset keeps a record of those file changes and their relevant references. It also keeps the parent information and author details. Here, “changed files” doesn’t mean a sequence of line-by-line patches.

A merge can also have multiple parents. The first parent gives you the baseline against which Scion records its file changes.

Changeset metadata is stored in Spanner, which is a distributed database. Compressed file contents are kept in cloud object storage. The root tree is derived by the server rather than being stored directly inside the changeset.

This way, you can record a change based on the changed data and affected structures. No need to process the whole repository.

How Scion Caches Data

Using immutable objects makes it easy to use shared caching.

Scion recognizes its source control objects by their contents. This technique is known as content-addressing. In this approach, you have a hash function that calculates an identifier from the contents of an object. The system can then find that object later using this identifier. If there’s a change in the content, the new object gets a different ID value.

This way, your stored objects are immutable. A specific ID continues to refer to the same data. For example, let’s say you have a cache that contains a particular version of “parser[dot].rs”. If you have another job that asks for the same object, the cache can return it without asking another server if the contents have been modified. If there’s a new version of the file, it means the object is different.

There are two consequences of this. One is that you can use identical content. Cached historical objects don’t need freshness checks merely because development is happening somewhere else in the repository.

Git uses content addressing. But the way Scion differs is in how extensively its service and architecture are organized around asking for and caching these objects.

Information still changes in the system. For example, let’s say the name “main” moves as changes are integrated. The immutable object that represents a specific version and the mutable name that identifies the latest version require you to treat things differently.

How Anthropic Scales Scion

Scion scales by combining shared source control APIs with a hierarchy of caches. Its design is such that answering questions is separate from delivering the files needed for a working directory.

The first point is that repository operations move into a shared service. Many tools need information such as which changes affected a file, who modified a line, and so on. If you’ve to maintain a local repository to answer such questions, it creates a lot of downloading and maintenance work.

Scion exposes these operations through APIs. You can have clients ask the servers directly. The servers can compute derived data when needed and save those results to Spanner. With this, any jobs that only need these answers don’t have to prepare a local repository.

Second, you have immutable objects that make caching pretty simple. As we saw earlier, Scion identifies objects using hashes based on their contents. An existing ID always refers to the same data.

Third, clients only request the objects they need. Scion represents directory structure through trees and file contents through blobs. The client identifies what is missing. So the server receives explicit object requests rather than having to think about a customized transfer.

Fourth, by sharing caches, they reduce the need for repeated downloads and computation. On a compute node, jobs talk to “scion-daemon”. You can think of it as a background process that shares cached objects across jobs.

Any missing objects come from “scion-cache”. This is the regional caching layer that’s shared across many nodes. If that layer also misses, you can get the data from authoritative Scion servers that read from Spanner or cloud storage.

Lastly, you also have strict cache boundaries that help contain failures. All three layers support the same object-request interface. Otherwise, a regional cache that fails could cause its consumers to overwhelm the authoritative servers.

Conclusion

The Anthropic engineering team learnt a lot of important lessons while building and running Scion.

First was that rapid development is very possible with a small team. For reference, it was just a team of seven people that built both Scion and Antique (which is their code review tool).

The second takeaway was that developers are still valuable, but their scope of work is changing. All of the developers working on this system would rate Claude as better at writing code than they are. But the developers were critical in providing invaluable understanding of the high-level inter-system components and considering the trade-offs in the design decisions. A lot of the developer work revolved around stopping Claude from taking a certain path.

Third, they were able to make things more optimized and also deliver high-quality stuff. Due to Claude’s ability to write a ton of code much faster than human developers, Scion is among the most well-tested and well-defended codebases they’ve ever created.

Fourth, they were able to achieve a new level of operational excellence. The team uses Claude Tag heavily so that they can monitor each component of the system.
